Turkish and Syrian government forces came into direct military confrontation when a Syrian airstrike killed 34 Turkish soldiers in February 2020. A ceasefire brokered by Russia and Turkey halted the offensive, leaving Idlib divided.

title: Caesar Act Sanctions Devastate Syrian Economy
description: The Caesar Syria Civilian Protection Act, passed by the US Congress and signed into law in December 2019, came into effect in June 2020, imposing sweeping secondary sanctions targeting anyone — including third-country companies — that did business with the Assad government. The sanctions effectively blocked Syria's economic reconstruction, preventing foreign companies from participating in rebuilding projects. Critics argued the measures disproportionately harmed ordinary Syrians; proponents said the regime should not profit from reconstruction without accountability.

title: Syrian Pound Collapses Amid Multiple Economic Crises
description: The Syrian pound entered a free-fall in 2020, losing more than 80% of its value against the dollar as the cumulative effects of war destruction, sanctions, capital flight, the Lebanese financial crisis (which trapped Syrian deposits in Lebanese banks), and COVID-19 devastated the economy. Inflation made basic goods unaffordable for most Syrians, including in government-held areas. The economic collapse eroded whatever remaining popular support the regime retained among its urban base.

title: Deraa Uprising Reignites: Regime Besieges Birthplace of Revolution
description: The city of Deraa — where the 2011 uprising began — rose again in 2021 when residents resisted a government security crackdown, leading to a months-long siege by Syrian military and Russian forces. Former rebel fighters who had accepted reconciliation agreements rose up against arbitrary arrests and security pressures. A negotiated settlement eventually ended the siege, but the episode demonstrated that the regime's 'reconciliation' in southern Syria was fragile and resentment remained deep.

title: Syrian Presidential Election: Assad Claims Implausible Victory
description: Hafez al-Assad held presidential elections in May 2021, claiming 95.1 percent of the vote in what Western governments and human rights organizations dismissed as a fraudulent exercise in authoritarian theater. The election was held only in government-controlled areas and excluded millions of displaced Syrians. No credible international observers were permitted. The exercise was widely seen as an effort to demonstrate regime normality while the country remained devastated by war.

title: Iran Deepens Economic and Military Footprint in Syria
description: Iran consolidated its military and economic presence in Syria in 2021, establishing permanent military bases, acquiring commercial licenses, and extending credit lines that gave Tehran significant leverage over Damascus. Iranian-backed militia networks — including Hezbollah, Kata'ib Hezbollah, and others — maintained positions across southern and eastern Syria. Israel continued conducting airstrikes against Iranian military infrastructure in Syria, sometimes killing Iranian Revolutionary Guard commanders.

title: Arab League Moves to Readmit Syria as Regional Normalization Advances
description: Several Arab states — led by the UAE, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia — began a process of normalizing diplomatic relations with Assad's Syria in 2022-2023, ending the isolation imposed after 2011. The normalization was driven partly by pragmatic acceptance of Assad's survival, partly by desire to reduce Iranian influence in Syria, and partly by pressure to address the refugee crisis. The Arab League formally readmitted Syria in May 2023, though critics argued the move rewarded Assad without accountability.

title: ISIS Resurrects Major Attack on Ghwayran Prison in Hasakah
description: ISIS launched its most ambitious operation in years in January 2022, attacking the Ghwayran prison in Hasakah — the largest ISIS detention facility in northeastern Syria — in an attempt to free thousands of imprisoned fighters. The attack, which killed more than 500 people over ten days of fighting, demonstrated ISIS's continued organizational capacity and the dangerous overcrowding of detention facilities holding ISIS members. US and SDF forces eventually suppressed the assault.

title: Major Earthquake Devastates Aleppo, Hama, and Idlib
description: A devastating magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck southern Turkey and northwestern Syria on February 6, 2023, killing more than 6,000 Syrians and leaving hundreds of thousands homeless in the already devastated rebel-held northwest. Thousands of buildings collapsed on sleeping residents in the pre-dawn hours. The Assad government initially restricted humanitarian access across conflict lines, drawing sharp international criticism. Eventually some border crossings were opened, but the political complications delayed the delivery of aid.

title: Syria-Turkey Normalization Talks Stall Over Troop Withdrawal Demand
description: Russian-mediated talks between Syria and Turkey aimed at normalizing their relationship — shattered by Turkey's support for rebel groups — stalled repeatedly over Ankara's demand that Syrian refugees return home and Damascus's insistence that Turkey withdraw its military forces from northern Syria. Erdogan's desire for refugee return before the 2023 Turkish elections created a diplomatic push, but Assad refused to offer the security guarantees Turkey sought for returning refugees.

title: Syrian Drug Trade: Captagon Becomes Major Regime Revenue Source
description: Syria under Assad became the world's leading producer and exporter of captagon — an amphetamine-type stimulant — with production and distribution networks closely linked to regime figures, particularly Maher al-Assad's Fourth Armored Division. Captagon exports to Gulf states, Jordan, and beyond generated estimated revenues of billions of dollars annually, becoming a significant source of funding for the regime amid sanctions. The US and Gulf states enacted specific legislation targeting Syrian captagon networks.

title: HTS Launches Lightning Offensive, Capturing Aleppo in Days
description: In late November 2024, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) — the dominant rebel group in Idlib — launched a surprise offensive and captured Aleppo within days, shocking a Syrian government military that had grown complacent after years of stalemate. The speed of the HTS advance — aided by other rebel factions — exposed the hollowness of Assad's military despite Russian and Iranian backing. The fall of Aleppo began the rapid unraveling of the Assad regime.

title: Assad Regime Collapses: Bashar Flees to Russia
description: In a stunning sequence of events in December 2024, rebel forces swept from Aleppo through Hama and Homs to Damascus in less than two weeks. On December 8, 2024, Syrian state media confirmed that Bashar al-Assad had fled the country — reportedly to Russia — and the regime effectively collapsed. After 53 years of Assad family rule, the Ba'athist state disintegrated with barely a fight, as military units melted away and security services abandoned their posts. HTS leader Ahmad al-Sharaa entered Damascus as opposition forces took control of the capital; crowds celebrated in the streets and political prisoners were freed from the notorious Sednaya prison.

title: Sednaya Prison Opened: Scale of Horror Revealed
description: When rebel forces liberated Sednaya Prison — Assad's most feared detention facility — near Damascus, survivors and investigators encountered evidence of systematic torture, mass executions, and inhumane conditions that shocked the world. Human rights organizations documented that tens of thousands of Syrians had disappeared into Sednaya and similar facilities over the decades of Assad rule, many never seen again. The prison became a symbol of the regime's crimes against its own people.

title: Israeli Forces Seize Buffer Zone and Advance Into Syrian Territory
description: Taking advantage of the Assad regime's collapse, Israeli forces moved across the UN buffer zone in the Golan Heights and advanced into Syrian territory, capturing strategic hills overlooking Damascus. Israel described the moves as temporary defensive measures to prevent weapons falling into hostile hands. The advance provoked international criticism and raised questions about Israel's long-term intentions toward post-Assad Syria.

title: Russia and Iran Lose Their Syrian Anchor
description: The fall of Assad delivered a major strategic blow to Russia and Iran, both of which had invested massively in preserving the regime. Russia's Tartus naval base — its only Mediterranean naval facility — and Hmeimim Air Base came under negotiation. Iran lost its primary Arab state ally and the land corridor to Hezbollah in Lebanon. The collapse forced both powers to rapidly reassess their Middle East strategies.

title: HTS-Led Transitional Authority Establishes Interim Government
description: Ahmad al-Sharaa (Abu Mohammad al-Jolani) and HTS established a transitional governing authority in Damascus, appointing a technocratic prime minister and beginning the work of assembling a national unity government. The process was complicated by the multiplicity of armed factions operating across Syria, Turkish-backed groups in the north, Kurdish autonomous administration in the northeast, and the sheer scale of Syria's state collapse. International engagement — including from Western governments and Gulf states — began cautiously.

title: International Community Debates Lifting Syria Sanctions
description: With Assad gone, Western governments faced pressure to lift the Caesar Act sanctions and other economic restrictions to enable Syrian reconstruction and refugee return. Advocates argued that sanctions had hurt ordinary Syrians and now had no deterrent purpose. Critics insisted on conditionality — accountability for war crimes and genuine political transition. The debate unfolded against the backdrop of Syria's catastrophic economic situation and the urgent need for reconstruction.

title: Syrian Refugees Face Complex Return Questions
description: The fall of Assad raised hopes for the return of millions of Syrian refugees — an estimated 5-6 million in Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, and Europe — but the reality proved far more complicated. Security conditions in many parts of Syria remained precarious, housing and infrastructure were destroyed, and minority communities feared reprisals. Turkey pressed for rapid mass returns, while European governments conditioned normalization of relations on verified safe conditions. Some refugees began returning voluntarily while others waited.

title: Kurdish Autonomous Authority Negotiates Future Status
description: The Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria (AANES), governing roughly a third of Syrian territory, entered negotiations with the transitional government in Damascus over its future status. Kurds sought constitutional recognition of their autonomy, protection of Kurdish cultural and linguistic rights, and integration of their forces into a future national army. Turkey remained deeply hostile to any formalized Kurdish autonomy and continued military pressure in the north.

title: War Crimes Accountability: Investigations and Documentation Begin
description: International and Syrian civil society organizations accelerated efforts to document and prosecute war crimes committed during Syria's 14-year civil war, with evidence gathered under universal jurisdiction laws in European courts. The Caesar Files — photographs smuggled out by a Syrian military defector documenting 11,000 torture victims — became central evidence in ongoing proceedings. Survivors and victims' families demanded accountability for crimes committed by both the Assad regime and extremist groups.

title: Reconstruction Challenge: Syria Faces Decades of Rebuilding
description: Assessments of Syria's reconstruction needs produced staggering figures — estimates ranged from $250 billion to $400 billion over decades to rebuild the country's destroyed housing, infrastructure, hospitals, schools, and industry. The Syrian economy had contracted by more than 60 percent since 2011, poverty was near-universal, and a generation of children had grown up without adequate education. The scale of the reconstruction challenge dwarfed available resources and tested the international community's commitment.
